title: Experimental study of the effect of fonts on fluency and word recall in a second language
abstract: Context and relevance. Previous studies have identified changes in cognitive processes when disfluency is introduced (increased metacognitive estimates of cognitive processing difficulty). However, these studies have scarcely examined the effects of disfluency on second language learning. Objective. The present study focuses on experimentally testing the effects of font on fluency and foreign language word memorisation. Methods and materials. The study was conducted in a group of participants (N = 304; 62% female; mean age = 18.28) learning English as a foreign language. The participants' task was to memorise pairs of English words presented in either easy (Arial and Arial bold) or hard-to-read fonts (Sans Forgetica, a specially designed font that disrupts perceptual fluency by removing parts of letters and slanting). The participants were asked to reproduce the pairs by the first word a few minutes after memorisation and 2 weeks after memorisation. The number of correctly reproduced pairs was recorded. Results. The findings indicated that participants preferred the easy font over the hard-to-read font, suggesting a preference for ease of processing. However, the study revealed that the font did not influence the memorisation of foreign language words. Conclusions. The study's findings are consistent with those of previous disfluency research conducted on native language materials. At this stage, the use of hard-to-read fonts in educational practice is not recommended for disfluency induction.
